title: Four Republicans Cross Party Lines As US House Votes To Limit Trump's Iran War Powers
text:
World
Kuldeep Negi
Jun 04, 2026 | Updated 10:00 AM GMT+5:30
Save & read from anywhere!

The US House of Representatives today (4 June) delivered a stinging rebuke to President Donald Trump, passing a war powers resolution directing him to end military hostilities with Iran.
The measure passed by a vote of 215 to 208, with four Republicans joining Democrats in support, marking the first time such a measure has cleared the House or the Senate on a final vote since the start of the conflict more than three months ago.
Republican Representatives Thomas Massie, Brian Fitzpatrick, Tom Barrett and Warren Davidson crossed party lines to support the resolution.
Massie, a Kentucky Republican, explained his vote by citing constituent frustration, stating people were tired of expensive fuel and fertiliser costs linked to the war.
Fitzpatrick defended his decision as following the 1973 War Powers Act, noting the 60-day threshold had expired.
The resolution directs Trump to remove US armed forces from hostilities with Iran, unless Congress votes to declare war or authorises using military force against it.
The conflict began on 28 February with strikes by US and Israeli forces on Iran, and at least 13 US soldiers have been killed in the conflict, which spilled into nearby countries, whilst more than 3,400 people have died in Iran during the war.
Speaker Mike Johnson opposed the measure, warning it would weaken Trump's negotiating position.
The resolution had originally been set for a vote two weeks ago, but Republican leaders sent House members home early for a May recess when it appeared the largely Democratic-backed measure had enough Republican votes for passage. The delay failed to shift support.
While largely symbolic, the vote represents mounting Congressional frustration with the unpopular war.
The vote marked the fourth time this year that the House has voted on a war powers resolution, with previous attempts failing narrowly.
The resolution now proceeds to the Senate, though Trump is likely to veto any attempt to curtail his military powers, and only a bill passed with a two-thirds majority in both the House and Senate can overcome a presidential veto.
Kuldeep is Senior Editor (Newsroom) at Swarajya. He tweets at @kaydnegi.
